title: Seasonal Creative Belongs in Your Digital Signage Strategy
summary: Seasonal moments drive retail sales. Learn how digital signage keeps creative fresh, supports retail media networks, and helps screens pay for themselves.
body_markdown:
November and December have averaged about


[19% of annual retail sales](https://nrf.com/research-insights/holiday-data-and-trends/winter-holidays/winter-holiday-faqs) over the last five years, according to the National Retail Federation. Shoppers arrive ready to buy, and brands arrive ready to reach them. Per NRF, roughly two in five holiday shoppers start shopping before November, so the season begins earlier than the calendar says. Yet plenty of in-store screens still run their July loop in December, and shoppers have learned to look right past them.


Timely creative wins that attention back. In Mood Media’s 2025 holiday survey,


[56% of shoppers](https://us.moodmedia.com/blog/how-sensory-design-is-reshaping-seasonal-shopping/) said they noticed seasonal digital signage content. A screen that reflects the moment gets noticed. One that ignores the season gets ignored.


## A Stale Screen Costs Money


Every day a screen shows last month’s offer, it wastes prime real estate on a message that no longer fits. A Halloween promo that lingers into Thanksgiving confuses guests. A holiday item that sold out Saturday but still plays on Sunday frustrates them. Each one costs a sale or a little trust, and in the busiest weeks of the year they add up fast.


### Printed Signage Can’t Keep Up with the Calendar


Printed signage locks a message in place for weeks. Every seasonal change means designing, printing, shipping, and installing new materials at every location, then removing them on time. When there are hundreds of stores to manage, someone is always a few days behind.


[Digital signage solutions](https://cri.com/what-we-do/digital-signage-solutions?hsLang=en) remove those steps and do things print can’t.


- Updates go live everywhere at once. A new holiday promotion, price, or jackpot can publish from one content management system to every screen in minutes.


- Campaigns start and stop on schedule. Scheduled playlists launch seasonal content on time and retire it automatically.


- Messages follow time of day and location. Dayparting serves breakfast, lunch or late-night offers when they matter, and regional pricing zones let one campaign adapt to local markets.


- Creative can move. An animated, full-screen spot for a limited-time peppermint or pumpkin drink grabs guests before they reach the menu. A static poster can’t do that.


- Screens react in real time. Connected to point-of-sale and inventory data, they can update prices, promote what’s in stock, and discount items before they expire.


- Results are easier to measure. Content runs on a schedule tied to sales data, so retailers and advertisers can see which seasonal flights moved product.


For


[retail](https://cri.com/who-we-serve/retail?hsLang=en) brands, that speed matters most when traffic peaks and offers change daily.


## For Retail Media Networks, Seasons Are Inventory


Holidays, weather shifts, and cultural moments are inventory brands want to buy. Limited-time offers create urgency, in-store messages connect to products shoppers can take home, and advertisers get a timely reason to show up at the point of purchase. A retail media network that can’t turn with the season has less to sell.


### Plan It Like a Program


Seasonal creative pays off when the network keeps up with the calendar. Brands and retailers need to launch holiday campaigns on time, adjust prices and promotions as demand shifts, and pull outdated messages the moment a season ends.


The strongest programs start early and follow the same steps each season:


1.


Map the year’s moments, including holidays, local events, weather turns, and product launches.


2.


Produce creative in batches for each moment.


3.


Schedule creative before each flight begins, and leave room to adjust, because demand rarely follows the forecast.


4.


Measure every flight. Compare content against sales data and note which offers and formats moved product.


5.


Apply what worked to next season’s plan.


A quick-service restaurant can retire a sold-out limited-time drink by lunch, and a lottery can publish a jackpot change the minute it happens. Each season then gives the next one a head start.
